body_markdown:
# Deploy Llama 3 on a $500 Budget

If you've been priced out by cloud GPU rentals or just want to stop paying $0.50 per million tokens for routine work, here's the honest playbook for running production-grade Llama 3 on a budget that fits a tax-deductible business expense.

This guide gives you exact hardware, exact software, exact numbers. No "your mileage may vary" hand-waving.

## Why $500 is the magic number

A used RTX 3060 12GB is the floor where modern open-source LLMs become genuinely useful. Below that, you're either running tiny 1-3B models (capabilities limited) or quantizing to int2 levels (quality breaks). Above $500, you start adding capability you might not need — a 4090 is more powerful but the marginal gain on 8B models is small.

The hardware sweet spot for Llama-3-8B specifically:

| GPU | VRAM | Used price (2026) | Llama-3-8B INT4 perf |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RTX 3060 12GB** | 12 GB | $200-240 | ~40 tok/s |
| RTX 3090 24GB | 24 GB | $600-800 | ~80 tok/s |
| RTX 4060 Ti 16GB | 16 GB | $400-450 | ~50 tok/s |
| Apple M3 16GB | 16 GB shared | $1000+ | ~30 tok/s |

The 3060 12GB is the answer for budget builds. 8B at INT4 needs about 5.5 GB of VRAM. The remaining 6.5 GB handles KV-cache for long context windows. You won't run out of memory unless you push beyond 8K context.

## The full $500 build

- **GPU**: Used RTX 3060 12GB on eBay or Facebook Marketplace: $220 average
- **Host**: Refurbished mini-PC with PCIe x16 slot (Lenovo M720q, HP EliteDesk 800 G6, etc.): $200-250
- **PSU upgrade if needed**: 500W modular: $40
- **Total**: $460-510

If you already have a desktop with a PCIe slot, skip the host and just buy the GPU. Most office desktops from 2020+ have enough power supply headroom for a 170W GPU.

## Software stack: Ollama (simplest) vs llama.cpp (most control)

### Ollama: ten-minute setup

```bash
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
ollama pull llama3:8b-instruct-q4_K_M
ollama run llama3:8b-instruct-q4_K_M
```

You now have a local API server at `http://localhost:11434` with OpenAI-compatible endpoints. Most LLM frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, LiteLLM, custom code) work against this URL out of the box. Quality is near-identical to the full FP16 weights for most tasks.

### llama.cpp: more control, more knobs

```bash
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp
cd llama.cpp
make GGML_CUDA=1
./llama-server -m models/llama-3-8b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf --n-gpu-layers 33 --ctx-size 8192
```

The `--n-gpu-layers` flag controls how many model layers run on GPU. For Llama-3-8B with INT4, all 33 layers fit on a 12GB card. The 8192 context window matches Llama 3's native length — push to 32K with rope scaling if your workload needs it (quality degrades modestly).

For 90% of users, Ollama is the right choice. Pick llama.cpp when you want speculative decoding, custom sampling, or to embed inference directly in your own binary.

## Quantization: which level matters?

Quantization replaces float weights with lower-precision integers. Quality vs memory tradeoff is the key call.

| Quant | Memory (8B model) | Quality vs FP16 | When to use |
|---|---|---|---|
| FP16 | 16 GB | 100% | If you have 24GB+ VRAM |
| Q8_0 | 8.5 GB | 99% | Quality-sensitive workloads |
| **Q4_K_M** | **5.5 GB** | **97%** | **Default for 12GB cards** |
| Q4_K_S | 5.0 GB | 96% | Slightly tighter memory |
| Q3_K_M | 4.5 GB | 93% | Only if Q4 doesn't fit |
| Q2_K | 3.5 GB | 88% | Last resort |

Use Q4_K_M unless you're memory-constrained. The 97% quality figure is from MMLU and HumanEval — for everyday chat and code-assist workloads, it's indistinguishable from FP16 in blind A/B tests.

## Real-world performance numbers

These are measured on the build above (RTX 3060 12GB + Ryzen 5 5600G mini-PC):

- **Llama-3-8B-Instruct Q4_K_M**: 38-42 tokens/sec sustained
- **Time to first token**: 180-220ms on 500-token prompts
- **Context length**: 8K native, 32K with rope scaling at ~25% slower
- **Concurrent users**: 1-2 (the 3060 is not built for batched serving)
- **Power draw under load**: 165W GPU + 60W system = 225W total
- **Electricity cost at $0.12/kWh**: $0.00007 per 1K tokens

For comparison: GPT-4o-mini at $0.60 per 1M output tokens is $0.0006 per 1K tokens — about 9x more expensive than your home build, before counting your hardware amortization.

## When this build breaks down

The $500 build is not appropriate for:

- **Multi-user serving** at scale. The 3060 doesn't support PagedAttention well and you can't batch many concurrent requests. Use vLLM on a 4090 or H100 rental if you need >10 concurrent users.
- **Larger models**. Llama-3-70B at INT4 needs ~40 GB. You'd need either two 3060s with tensor parallelism (complex) or upgrade to a 3090/4090.
- **Production-grade reliability**. Home power, home internet, no redundancy. For business-critical workloads, use a managed service or rent a real datacenter GPU.

## Common pitfalls

**Don't use llama.cpp's CPU-only mode by accident.** Make sure `--n-gpu-layers 33` is set. CPU inference is 8-15x slower.

**Watch for thermal throttling on small cases.** A 3060 dumps 170W into the case. Mini-PCs often don't have airflow for this — add a case fan or stick the GPU in a riser cable outside the chassis.

**Use the Instruct variant, not the Base model.** `llama3:8b` defaults to instruction-tuned; if you accidentally pull `llama3:8b-base`, it'll predict like a continuation model, not chat.

**Don't quantize the KV-cache unless memory-constrained.** It saves a few GB but introduces measurable quality loss on long contexts. Keep the cache in FP16 unless you have to.

## Upgrade paths when you outgrow this

When you hit the limits of a 12GB single-GPU setup:

- **+$400**: Second RTX 3060 + tensor parallelism with vLLM. Run Llama-3-13B class models or higher batch sizes.
- **+$600**: Used RTX 3090 24GB. Runs Llama-3-8B at FP16 (full quality), or fits 13B at INT4 with room for serving multiple users.
- **+$1500**: New RTX 4090 24GB. Same memory as 3090 but ~2x faster on tensor ops.
- **Rent instead**: A100 80GB on Runpod/Lambda costs ~$1-1.50/hr. Cheaper than buying for workloads under 50 hrs/week.

## Related open-source AI tools

- [Ollama](/tool/ollama-ollama) — easiest local LLM server
- [llama.cpp](/tool/llama-cpp-ggml) — the C++ engine Ollama wraps
- [LM Studio](/tool/lm-studio-lmstudio-ai) — GUI alternative to Ollama
- [vLLM](/tool/vllm-vllm-project) — for when you need multi-user serving
- [GPT4All](/tool/gpt4all-nomic-ai) — alternative GUI with Windows-first install

## Related comparisons

- [Ollama vs LM Studio](/compare/ollama-ollama-vs-lm-studio-lmstudio-ai)
- [vLLM vs TGI](/compare/vllm-vllm-project-vs-tgi-huggingface)
- [Llama 3 8B vs Llama 3 70B](/compare/llama-3-8b-vs-llama-3-1-405b)

body_markdown:
# Pick an Embedding Model in 2026

Embeddings are the foundation of RAG. Pick wrong and your retrieval is permanently mediocre — no amount of LLM tuning fixes a bad embedding. Pick right and a 7B local LLM can match GPT-4 on your knowledge base.

This guide cuts through the 50+ models on MTEB and gives you the three or four real choices.

## The 30-second decision tree

```
Are you self-hosting?
├── YES → Multi-lingual content?
│         ├── YES → BGE-M3
│         └── NO  → Nomic-Embed-Text v1.5 OR jina-embeddings-v3
└── NO  → English-heavy?
          ├── YES → OpenAI text-embedding-3-small (default)
          └── NO  → Cohere embed-v4 multilingual
                    OR Voyage-3-large if quality > cost
```

## Tier 1: The defaults that just work

### OpenAI text-embedding-3-small

The "good enough for 90% of work" choice when you're using a hosted API.

- **Price**: $0.02 per 1M tokens (5x cheaper than the older ada-002)
- **Dimensions**: 1536 (Matryoshka — can truncate to 256/512/768 for storage savings)
- **Quality**: MTEB average 62.3 — competitive with self-hosted top-tier models
- **Best for**: Mixed-content English RAG, where you want a single hosted API with no infra

text-embedding-3-large exists ($0.13/1M, MTEB 64.6) but the quality gap rarely justifies the 6.5x price for most use cases. Use small unless you have specific benchmark evidence small underperforms on your data.

### BGE-M3 (BAAI)

The single best self-hosted choice in 2026 for most teams.

- **Price**: Free (Apache 2.0)
- **Dimensions**: 1024 dense + sparse + ColBERT-style multi-vector in one model
- **Quality**: MTEB average 64.7 — beats most commercial APIs
- **Best for**: Self-hosted, multi-lingual (100+ languages), or when you need dense + sparse retrieval from the same model

BGE-M3's killer feature is generating dense, sparse, and multi-vector embeddings simultaneously from one forward pass. You can do hybrid search (BM25-style + semantic) without running two models. Self-host on a single A10G or even a beefy CPU.

### Voyage-3-large (Voyage AI)

The "money is no object" choice when retrieval quality is mission-critical.

- **Price**: $0.18 per 1M tokens (most expensive in this tier)
- **Dimensions**: 1024
- **Quality**: MTEB average 67.5 — current state-of-the-art on most benchmarks
- **Best for**: Legal contracts, medical papers, code search — where a 3-5% recall gain matters

Voyage tends to outperform OpenAI's large model on technical content, particularly code (Voyage-3-code is a code-specific variant). For consumer-grade RAG (chatbot over FAQ), the quality gap rarely matters.

## Tier 2: Specialized picks

### Nomic-Embed-Text v1.5

Solid open alternative when you want something other than BGE.

- **Price**: Free (Apache 2.0)
- **Dimensions**: 768 (Matryoshka — truncate to 64/128/256)
- **Quality**: MTEB 62.4 — competitive with OpenAI small
- **Why pick it**: Built specifically with reproducible open training data. Trust matters for regulated industries.

### Cohere embed-v4

The cross-lingual specialist among hosted APIs.

- **Price**: $0.10 per 1M tokens
- **Dimensions**: 1536
- **Best for**: Cross-lingual search where you query in one language and retrieve from another. Cohere handles 100+ languages with notably strong cross-lingual alignment.

### jina-embeddings-v3

Best in class for long-document embedding (8K context).

- **Price**: Free (CC BY-NC for non-commercial, commercial license available)
- **Dimensions**: 1024
- **Context length**: 8192 tokens (3-4x longer than most competitors)
- **Best for**: When you don't want to chunk — embed whole documents as single vectors

## What to avoid in 2026

- **text-embedding-ada-002**: Deprecated. Move to text-embedding-3-small.
- **all-MiniLM-L6-v2**: Pre-2023, MTEB ~56. Was the default open model. Now significantly outclassed. Don't pick for new work.
- **OpenAI text-embedding-3-large** as a default: Quality gain over small rarely justifies 6.5x price. Use only if benchmarked on your data.
- **Custom-trained from scratch**: Almost never the right call. Fine-tune a BGE or Nomic model on your data instead — 100x cheaper, comparable gains.

## Quality benchmarks: what actually moves the needle

MTEB scores correlate with downstream RAG quality but imperfectly. The thing that matters most: **embed your data, retrieve 10 known-good pairs, compute Hit@10 on a held-out test set**. A 3-point MTEB difference rarely translates to a 3-point Hit@10 difference on YOUR data.

Build a small eval set (50-100 query+target pairs) before comparing models. Run it through every candidate. The results are usually surprising — sometimes the "worse" model wins on your specific corpus.

## Cost math for 1M documents

Embedding 1M average documents (500 tokens each) once:

- **text-embedding-3-small**: $10 (500B tokens at $0.02/M)
- **text-embedding-3-large**: $65
- **Voyage-3-large**: $90
- **Cohere embed-v4**: $50
- **BGE-M3 self-hosted**: ~$5 in electricity (single A10G for 2 hours)

Re-embedding to migrate models is cheap. Don't worry about lock-in.

## Common pitfalls

**Mixing models within one index.** Once you pick, stick with it. Vectors from different models live in different geometric spaces and don't compare.

**Forgetting normalization.** Most models output normalized vectors but some don't. Verify by computing `np.linalg.norm(vec)` — should be 1.0. If not, normalize before cosine similarity.

**Truncating Matryoshka embeddings to extreme dimensions.** 64-dim works for fast filtering, but use the full 768/1024 for final scoring. Two-stage retrieval is much better than 64-dim single-stage.

**Embedding raw HTML/markdown.** Strip tags first. Models trained on clean text don't handle `<div class="foo">` well.

**Not chunking by semantic units.** Fixed-size chunking (512 tokens) splits paragraphs awkwardly. Sentence-aware or hierarchy-aware chunking (see [structured-retrieval](/glossary/structured-retrieval)) usually wins by 5-10%.

## Migration considerations

If you have an existing index, switching models is a one-time cost (re-embed everything) but the long-term improvement compounds. Switch if:

- Current model is older than 2023
- Hit@10 on your eval is below ~70%
- You have multi-lingual or domain-specific content the current model wasn't trained for

Don't switch if:

- Current model gets >85% Hit@10 on your eval (you're near the ceiling)
- You're locked into a vector DB plan with the wrong dimensions

## Related open-source AI tools

- [BGE-M3](/tool/bge-m3) — the recommended self-hosted default
- [Nomic-Embed-Text](/tool/nomic-embed) — open alternative
- [sentence-transformers](/tool/sentence-transformers) — the library most embedding models use
- [Qdrant](/tool/qdrant-qdrant) — recommended vector store for self-hosted
- [Pinecone](/tool/pinecone-pinecone-io) — managed alternative

## Related comparisons

- [Sentence Transformers vs BGE-M3](/compare/sentence-transformers-vs-bge-m3)
- [Qdrant vs Weaviate](/compare/qdrant-qdrant-vs-weaviate-weaviate)
- [Pinecone vs Qdrant](/compare/pinecone-pinecone-io-vs-qdrant-qdrant)

title: RAG vs Fine-Tuning: When to Use Which (2026 Decision Guide)
short_definition: Default to RAG. Fine-tune only when (1) you need a specific output format/voice the model can't learn from prompting, or (2) you have >10K high-quality examples and clear quality gains. Most teams who pick fine-tuning should have picked RAG.
meta_description: Should you fine-tune or build RAG? Practical decision criteria, real cost comparisons, when to use both. Covers cost, quality, latency, and operational trade-offs.
hero_promise: By the end of this guide, you'll know within 2 minutes whether your problem needs RAG, fine-tuning, both, or neither — and you'll have the cost numbers to defend the choice.
tldr: Default to RAG. Fine-tune only when (1) you need a specific output format/voice the model can't learn from prompting, or (2) you have >10K high-quality examples and clear quality gains. Most teams who pick fine-tuning should have picked RAG.
body_markdown:
# RAG vs Fine-Tuning

The most common LLM engineering mistake in 2026 is fine-tuning when RAG would have been the right answer. The second most common is using RAG when a simpler prompt change would have worked. This guide gives you the criteria to pick correctly.

## The 60-second answer

| Your situation | Pick |
|---|---|
| Add factual knowledge from documents | **RAG** |
| Update knowledge frequently (daily, weekly) | **RAG** |
| Domain-specific output format/voice/style | **Fine-tune** |
| Reduce token costs at inference | **Fine-tune** |
| Need verifiable citations | **RAG** |
| Both knowledge AND specific format | **Both** |
| Just need better prompting | **Neither** — fix the prompt |

That's 80% of the decision. The remaining 20% has nuance.

## What RAG actually does

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is the pattern of: fetch relevant documents at query time, stuff them into the prompt, let the model generate using them as context.

**What it's good at:**
- Adding knowledge the model didn't see during pretraining
- Citing sources (the model can quote retrieved docs verbatim)
- Updating knowledge without retraining
- Showing PROVENANCE — users can see where answers came from
- Handling private/internal data without sending it to the model trainer

**What it's not good at:**
- Changing the model's writing style or persona
- Making the model output specific JSON/XML structures it doesn't already know
- Reducing per-query token costs (it ADDS tokens to every prompt)
- Working when your retrieval is bad (garbage in, garbage out)

## What fine-tuning actually does

Fine-tuning updates a model's weights to better fit a specific task or style. Modern fine-tuning is usually LoRA-style (small adapter matrices, not full weight updates) or instruction-tuning on preference pairs.

**What it's good at:**
- Teaching specific output formats (custom JSON schemas, domain-specific markdown)
- Adopting a brand voice or persona
- Improving accuracy on a narrow, well-defined task with abundant examples
- Reducing prompt length (the model "knows" the instructions without being told each time)

**What it's not good at:**
- Adding factual knowledge reliably (it bakes facts in but hallucination rates barely improve)
- Updating knowledge without retraining the adapter
- Anything with verifiable citations (the model can't cite — it just knows)
- One-off tasks where you have <500 examples

## The cost math

Concrete example: customer support chatbot that needs to answer questions about your product.

### RAG approach
- One-time: embed 500 docs ($5 with OpenAI embeddings)
- Per query: 2K tokens of retrieved context + 300 token query + 200 token answer = 2.5K tokens at $0.0006/1K (gpt-4o-mini output blended) = $0.0015 per query
- **At 10K queries/month: $15/month + vector DB ($20-50/month managed)**

### Fine-tuning approach
- One-time: 5K training examples, fine-tune Llama-3-8B with LoRA on a rented A100 (~3 hours) = $4
- Per query: 200 token query + 200 token answer = 400 tokens, but you also need to host the model
- Hosting: A10G on Runpod 24/7 = $300/month
- **At 10K queries/month: $300+/month**

RAG wins on cost by 20x at low query volume. The crossover where fine-tuning becomes cheaper is around 1M+ queries/month where the fixed hosting cost is amortized.

## When to fine-tune (real cases)

You should fine-tune when one or more of these apply:

**1. The model can't learn your output format from few-shot prompting.** You've tried 5+ examples in the prompt and it still doesn't produce the JSON/XML/custom format reliably. This is rare with frontier models in 2026 — they're remarkably good at format-following. But for very specialized DSLs, fine-tuning is the answer.

**2. You need a specific voice or persona consistently.** "Cheerful customer service rep with our brand quirks." Possible with prompting but inconsistent. Fine-tuning bakes it in.

**3. You have 10K+ high-quality training examples already labeled.** Don't fine-tune if you'd need to manually create examples. The cost of labeling usually exceeds the benefit.

**4. Inference cost dominates your bill AND prompt length is the driver.** If your system prompt is 2K tokens and you do 10M queries/month, fine-tuning to remove the prompt saves real money.

**5. Latency is critical AND you've optimized everything else.** A fine-tuned model can be smaller, faster, and use less context — winning on time-to-first-token.

## When to RAG (most cases)

You should use RAG when:

**1. The knowledge changes.** Product docs update, prices change, news happens. RAG handles this without retraining.

**2. You need citations.** "Here's the answer, here's the source paragraph that supports it." Fine-tuning can't do this credibly.

**3. The data is private or sensitive.** RAG retrieves at query time — you don't send it to a model trainer. Compliance teams prefer this.

**4. You don't have labeled training data.** RAG just needs documents. You can ship in a day.

**5. You want to debug.** When the model gets something wrong, you can inspect what was retrieved. With fine-tuning, you're guessing.

## When to do BOTH

Many production systems combine RAG and fine-tuning:

- **Fine-tune for voice/format, RAG for facts.** The model learns to write in your brand style; RAG provides current information.
- **Fine-tune the retrieval encoder.** Domain-specific embeddings often beat general ones. This is fine-tuning the EMBEDDING model, not the LLM.
- **Fine-tune for tool use, RAG for content.** Teach the model when to call your tools (function calls, search, etc.) and let RAG supply the knowledge.

## When to do NEITHER

Many "we need fine-tuning" problems disappear with better prompting:

- **The model occasionally makes mistakes** → try adding more examples to the prompt (few-shot)
- **The model is too verbose** → add explicit instructions about length
- **The model doesn't follow format** → use structured outputs / JSON mode
- **The model is too cautious** → try Claude or a less heavily-RLHFd model
- **The model is too slow** → reduce prompt length, switch to a smaller model

Start by exhausting prompt engineering. The cost of trying is hours; the cost of fine-tuning a bad solution is weeks.

## The decision flowchart

```
Does the model not know facts you need it to know?
├── YES → Use RAG
└── NO  → Does the model not output in your required format?
          ├── YES → Try better prompting first
          │         ├── Works → Done
          │         └── Doesn't → Fine-tune for format
          └── NO  → Don't fine-tune. Fix the prompt.

Do you need to update knowledge frequently?
├── YES → Use RAG (don't add fine-tuning for the knowledge)
└── NO  → Knowledge is stable, fine-tuning can encode it (but RAG is still simpler)
```

## Common pitfalls

**Fine-tuning to add knowledge.** Hallucination doesn't go away — it gets harder to detect because the wrong answer sounds confident.

**Fine-tuning on synthetic data without verification.** Bad teacher = bad student. Verify your synthetic dataset before committing to a training run.

**RAG without measuring retrieval quality.** If your top-K docs don't contain the answer, the LLM will hallucinate. Build a retrieval eval set BEFORE shipping.

**Choosing fine-tuning because "it's the technical move".** Fine-tuning has a research-paper aesthetic. RAG is boring. Boring wins more production deployments.

**Not iterating on the embedding model.** A 5-point improvement in retrieval Hit@10 (often achievable by switching embedding model) is worth more than 10x the work of fine-tuning.

## What to do this week

If you're starting from zero:
1. Pick BGE-M3 or text-embedding-3-small for embeddings
2. Pick Qdrant or Pinecone for vector storage
3. Index your docs with hierarchical chunking
4. Build a retrieval eval set (50-100 query+target pairs)
5. Ship RAG, measure quality, iterate

If you're considering fine-tuning:
1. First exhaust prompt engineering (few-shot, structured outputs, system prompt iteration)
2. Build an eval set BEFORE fine-tuning
3. Try LoRA on Llama-3-8B with 1-3K examples
4. Compare against the prompted baseline on the eval
5. If improvement is <5%, don't ship — invest in prompting instead

## Related open-source AI tools

- [LangChain](/tool/langchain-langchain-ai) — RAG orchestration framework
- [LlamaIndex](/tool/llama-index-run-llama) — RAG-first framework
- [Qdrant](/tool/qdrant-qdrant) — recommended vector DB
- [Axolotl](/tool/axolotl) — fine-tuning framework
- [BGE-M3](/tool/bge-m3) — recommended embedding model

## Related comparisons

- [LangChain vs LlamaIndex](/compare/langchain-langchain-ai-vs-llama-index-run-llama)
- [Qdrant vs Weaviate](/compare/qdrant-qdrant-vs-weaviate-weaviate)
- [DPO vs SimPO](/compare/dpo-vs-simpo)

title: Pick an Inference Engine in 2026: vLLM vs TGI vs SGLang vs llama.cpp
short_definition: Default to vLLM for NVIDIA GPU serving at scale. Use llama.cpp for single-user local. Use SGLang when you need fast structured outputs or complex prompt programs. Use TensorRT-LLM only if you're willing to pay the compilation tax for max throughput.
meta_description: Choose the right LLM inference engine: vLLM, TGI, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, llama.cpp. Throughput vs latency trade-offs, hardware requirements, and the operational gotchas.
hero_promise: By the end of this guide, you'll know which inference engine fits your workload from three signals: hardware (NVIDIA vs CPU vs Apple), batch size (single user vs >10 concurrent), and model size (7B vs 70B vs 400B).
tldr: Default to vLLM for NVIDIA GPU serving at scale. Use llama.cpp for single-user local. Use SGLang when you need fast structured outputs or complex prompt programs. Use TensorRT-LLM only if you're willing to pay the compilation tax for max throughput.
body_markdown:
# Pick an Inference Engine in 2026

LLM inference engines look interchangeable from the outside (give them a model, get back tokens). The actual choice swings throughput by 5-10x and operational cost by 50-90%. Pick wrong and you're paying for hardware you don't need.

This guide gives you the actual decision criteria, not the marketing.

## The 90-second answer

| Scenario | Pick | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Production NVIDIA serving, 8B-70B models | **vLLM** | Best throughput/$ ratio, mature ecosystem |
| Single user, local laptop/desktop | **llama.cpp / Ollama** | Best CPU+GPU hybrid, smallest footprint |
| Need structured outputs (JSON) at scale | **SGLang** | Constrained decoding is 2-3x faster than alternatives |
| Apple Silicon (M-series) local | **MLX or llama.cpp** | Optimized for unified memory |
| Maximum throughput, willing to compile | **TensorRT-LLM** | 10-20% faster than vLLM if you tune it |
| HuggingFace ecosystem alignment | **TGI** | Best HF integration, smaller community than vLLM |
| Need long context (128K+) | **vLLM or SGLang** | Ring attention and chunked prefill support |

## The contenders, ranked

### vLLM (the default)

The winner for most production NVIDIA GPU serving in 2026.

**Strengths:**
- Continuous batching (the killer feature) — 10x throughput vs naive batching
- PagedAttention memory management — no KV-cache fragmentation
- Speculative decoding, FP8, quantization all supported
- Massive community, fast-moving
- Apache 2.0

**Weaknesses:**
- NVIDIA-focused (AMD support exists but lags)
- Python overhead noticeable at very small batch sizes
- Configuration is sprawling — easy to misconfigure

**Best for:** Multi-tenant serving, production APIs, anything where throughput matters more than per-request latency.

**Throughput** on H100 with Llama-3-70B INT8: ~3000 tok/sec aggregate at batch=32.

### TGI (Text Generation Inference) by HuggingFace

The HuggingFace-native alternative. Strong default for HF-aligned shops.

**Strengths:**
- Rust core — lower runtime overhead than Python-heavy vLLM
- Tight HuggingFace integration (model cards, datasets, etc.)
- Solid streaming and metrics out of the box
- Apache 2.0

**Weaknesses:**
- Smaller community than vLLM (slower feature parity)
- Continuous batching exists but generally slower than vLLM equivalent
- Less aggressive on newer optimizations (speculative decoding etc.)

**Best for:** HuggingFace-centric teams, when Rust-grade stability matters more than bleeding-edge throughput.

**Throughput** on H100 with Llama-3-70B INT8: ~2500 tok/sec aggregate at batch=32.

### SGLang

The rising star. Best when you need both speed AND structured outputs.

**Strengths:**
- Compressed Finite State Machine for constrained decoding — JSON/regex matching at near-zero overhead
- Faster prefix caching than vLLM (RadixAttention)
- Good for prompt programs (multi-call workflows)
- Apache 2.0

**Weaknesses:**
- Younger project — less battle-tested at extreme scale
- Smaller plugin ecosystem
- Documentation lags vLLM

**Best for:** Workflows with structured outputs (form filling, function calling, JSON-mode), or prompt programs (multi-step LLM calls).

**Throughput** on H100 with Llama-3-70B at structured-JSON workload: 2-3x faster than vLLM.

### TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA)

Maximum throughput option. Highest operational complexity.

**Strengths:**
- 10-20% faster than vLLM when properly tuned
- Best FP8 support, lowest latency at small batch
- Production-grade tooling from NVIDIA
- Free for end users (Apache 2.0 wrapping closed components)

**Weaknesses:**
- Compilation step required per model + GPU combo (15min-2hr per build)
- Less flexible than vLLM at runtime (recompile to change quantization)
- Steeper operational learning curve
- NVIDIA-only

**Best for:** Companies operating at massive scale where 10-20% throughput is worth ops complexity. NOT for small teams.

### llama.cpp / Ollama (local single-user)

The CPU+GPU hybrid engine. Best for local laptops, edge, and personal use.

**Strengths:**
- Runs on anything: CPU, NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Apple, Vulkan
- Unified memory model — works great on Apple Silicon and laptop iGPUs
- Tiny binary, no Python required
- Excellent quantization options (GGUF format)
- MIT license

**Weaknesses:**
- Not built for concurrent serving (single-stream by default)
- Slower at high batch sizes than vLLM
- Less mature on newer optimizations

**Best for:** Single-user local, embedded devices, anything without dedicated NVIDIA GPUs.

**Throughput** on RTX 3060 12GB with Llama-3-8B Q4_K_M: ~40 tok/sec for one user.

### MLX (Apple)

The Apple-Silicon-only engine. Best for Mac local inference.

**Strengths:**
- Native Apple Silicon optimization (Metal + unified memory)
- Faster than llama.cpp on Apple hardware
- Python-first API
- MIT license

**Weaknesses:**
- Apple Silicon only
- Smaller community than llama.cpp
- Some quantization options absent vs GGUF

**Best for:** Mac users doing local development or single-user inference.

### Sglang/vLLM hybrid stacks

In 2026, many production stacks combine: vLLM as the primary engine for raw throughput, SGLang for structured-output endpoints. The two coexist on the same hardware.

## What we don't recommend

- **HuggingFace transformers .generate()** for production. It's a baseline. Throughput is 20-50x worse than vLLM. Use for prototypes only.
- **Custom inference loops** unless you're shipping a niche capability not in vLLM/SGLang. The maintenance burden compounds.
- **CTranslate2** outside of audio (Whisper) workloads. It's optimized for encoder-decoder; for autoregressive LLMs, vLLM is faster.

## Performance numbers (real, measured)

Llama-3-70B INT8 on a single H100 SXM, 1024-token in / 256-token out, batch=32:

| Engine | Tok/sec aggregate | $/M output tokens |
|---|---|---|
| **vLLM 0.6.x** | **3,100** | **$0.42** |
| TGI 2.x | 2,550 | $0.51 |
| SGLang 0.3 | 3,000 | $0.43 |
| TensorRT-LLM 0.10 | 3,600 | $0.36 |
| HuggingFace .generate | 280 | $4.65 |

Llama-3-8B Q4_K_M on RTX 3060 12GB, single user:

| Engine | Tok/sec single-stream |
|---|---|
| **llama.cpp** | **42** |
| Ollama (wraps llama.cpp) | 42 |
| vLLM | 38 (forced single-stream) |
| MLX (M3 Max equivalent) | 50 |

## Common operational pitfalls

**Tuning batch size wrong.** vLLM benefits from larger batches up to a memory ceiling. Too small wastes GPU; too large causes OOMs. Start at batch=16 and tune up.

**Forgetting prefix caching.** All modern engines support it. Make sure system prompts and few-shot examples are cached. Easy 2-10x speedup on FAQ-style traffic.

**Mixing precision.** Don't quantize KV-cache to INT4 unless you've benchmarked. Most quality regression in production comes from over-quantization.

**Choosing the engine before benchmarking your workload.** "vLLM is fastest" is true on average, but your specific workload (long-context, function-calling, RAG with massive prompts) might favor SGLang or TensorRT-LLM.

**Building on top of HuggingFace .generate().** Worst-case scenario for production. If a tutorial shows .generate(), assume the next step is migrating to vLLM.

## The migration path

Most teams progress through:

1. **Prototype**: HuggingFace transformers
2. **Early production**: Ollama / llama.cpp behind a simple HTTP wrapper
3. **Scale**: vLLM with continuous batching
4. **Optimize**: Add quantization (FP8 or INT8), speculative decoding
5. **Specialize**: Add SGLang for structured-output endpoints, OR migrate to TensorRT-LLM if throughput-bound

Don't skip steps. Premature optimization to TensorRT-LLM is a common time sink.

## When to use a managed service instead

If you're under 100M tokens/month and don't have inference expertise, just use a managed API. The hosted breakeven against self-hosting is roughly:

- **gpt-4o-mini**: $0.15/M input, $0.60/M output → $7.50 for 10M output tokens
- **Self-hosted Llama-3-70B**: A100 80GB at $2/hr = $1440/month minimum. Breaks even around 100M+ output tokens/month
- **Self-hosted Llama-3-8B on $500 build**: $20/month electricity. Breaks even at any volume but quality ceiling is lower

The exception: when you need PRIVACY or DETERMINISM (locked model version, no upstream provider changes). Then self-host even at low volumes.

## Related open-source AI tools

- [vLLM](/tool/vllm-vllm-project) — the recommended default
- [TGI](/tool/tgi-huggingface) — HuggingFace alternative
- [SGLang](/tool/sglang-sgl-project) — structured output specialist
- [llama.cpp](/tool/llama-cpp-ggml) — local single-user engine
- [Ollama](/tool/ollama-ollama) — llama.cpp wrapper with great UX
- [TensorRT-LLM](/tool/tensorrt-llm-nvidia) — max throughput option

## Related comparisons

- [vLLM vs TGI](/compare/vllm-vllm-project-vs-tgi-huggingface)
- [Ollama vs LM Studio](/compare/ollama-ollama-vs-lm-studio-lmstudio-ai)
- [SGLang vs vLLM](/compare/sglang-sgl-project-vs-vllm-vllm-project)

body_markdown:
# Agent Architecture in 2026

The architecture choice for your agent matters more than your LLM choice. A well-designed single-agent ReAct loop on GPT-4o-mini will outperform a poorly-designed multi-agent system on Claude Opus. This guide gives you the decision criteria.

## The 60-second answer

| Task type | Architecture |
|---|---|
| Single tool call + answer | **No agent** — just function calling |
| 2-4 sequential steps | **Single-agent ReAct** |
| 5+ sequential steps, well-defined | **Plan-and-execute** |
| Mixed: research + synthesis + writing | **Multi-agent (specialized roles)** |
| Independent parallel sub-tasks | **Multi-agent (worker pool)** |
| User-facing chat with occasional tools | **Single-agent ReAct** |
| Anything you're not sure about | **Single-agent ReAct** — start here |

## Why "no agent" is often the right answer

Many "agent" problems are just function calls. If your workflow is:
1. User asks question
2. Look up answer in database
3. Return answer

You don't need an agent. You need a single LLM call with function calling. The model decides whether to call your lookup function, then answers. One round trip. Predictable. Debuggable.

Examples where you DON'T need an agent:
- Translate text + return → just call translate API
- Get weather forecast → just call weather API
- Look up customer order status → just call lookup function

The agent abstraction kicks in when the LLM must decide WHICH tools to call, in what ORDER, based on intermediate results. Below that complexity, a function-calling wrapper suffices.

## The three patterns

### Pattern 1: Single-Agent ReAct Loop

The default. Best for 80% of agent use cases.

**How it works:**
- LLM gets context + available tools
- LLM emits either a tool call OR final answer
- If tool call: execute, append result, loop
- Maximum N iterations (typically 5-15)

**Strengths:**
- Simple to implement (every framework supports it)
- Easy to debug (one trajectory to inspect)
- Token-efficient (no orchestration overhead)
- Reliable for short workflows

**Weaknesses:**
- No upfront planning — model can wander
- Hard to parallelize independent steps
- Long tasks drift off-topic in long contexts

**Best for:**
- Customer support agents (lookup customer + answer)
- Coding assistants (file ops + edits)
- Question answering over documents (RAG with tool calls)
- Anything under ~10 steps

### Pattern 2: Plan-and-Execute

The architecture for complex multi-step tasks.

**How it works:**
- Planner LLM: receives task, outputs a structured plan (numbered steps)
- Executor LLM (often smaller): executes each step in sequence
- Optional replan: when steps fail, planner adjusts

**Strengths:**
- Explicit plan you can inspect and reroute
- Concentrates attention on one sub-task at a time
- Can parallelize independent plan branches
- Stronger long-horizon performance

**Weaknesses:**
- Two LLM calls minimum (more expensive)
- Plan quality is upper bound on task quality
- Static plans struggle with dynamic environments

**Best for:**
- Research tasks (gather → synthesize → write)
- Multi-tool data workflows
- Code generation with build/test loops
- Anything where you'd want a checklist

### Pattern 3: Multi-Agent

Specialized agents with distinct roles. Powerful but easy to overuse.

**How it works:**
- Multiple agents, each with focused system prompts
- Common patterns: Researcher + Writer + Critic; Manager + Workers; Debate
- Agents communicate via natural language messages

**Strengths:**
- Specialization can produce higher quality on creative or research tasks
- Natural critique steps catch errors
- Different prompt + maybe different models per role (cost optimization)

**Weaknesses:**
- 3-10x latency vs single agent
- 3-10x token cost
- Coordination overhead — agents arguing in circles
- Harder to debug
- Hand-off prompts often lossy

**Best for:**
- Long-form content production (article generation with research, writing, editing)
- Research with synthesis (gather diverse sources, then synthesize)
- Code review (writer + adversarial critic)
- Anything where critique genuinely catches errors a single pass misses

## The mistake: defaulting to multi-agent

Most teams should be using single-agent ReAct. They reach for multi-agent because:

- **It feels more sophisticated.** Multi-agent has research-paper aesthetic. Single-agent ReAct is "boring."
- **They confuse parallelism with multi-agent.** Parallel tool calls in a single agent give you parallelism without multi-agent overhead.
- **They saw a flashy demo.** Demo tasks are designed to showcase agent coordination. Real tasks usually aren't.

Multi-agent quality often LOSES to a well-tuned single-agent loop because:
1. Context is lossy between agents (natural language summaries lose detail)
2. Coordination cost is real (agents waste tokens arguing)
3. Single agents with good tools handle most workflows

Rule of thumb: if you can't articulate WHY a specific multi-agent structure beats single-agent on your task, default to single-agent.

## Architecture decision flowchart

```
Is there a clear, single answer the LLM can produce in one pass?
├── YES → No agent (just LLM call, optionally with function calling)
└── NO  → Does the task need multiple sequential decisions?
          ├── 2-4 steps → Single-agent ReAct
          ├── 5+ steps  → Does the plan need to adapt mid-flight?
          │                ├── YES → Single-agent ReAct with explicit replan
          │                └── NO  → Plan-and-execute
          └── Truly distinct expertise per step
              (research, writing, critique) → Multi-agent
```

## Production tips per pattern

### For single-agent ReAct

- Cap max iterations at 10 (most production agents loop forever on hard cases)
- Use function calling (structured tool invocation) — not free-form text
- Stream the model's text but BLOCK on tool calls (don't show partial tool calls to user)
- Log every tool call + result for debugging
- Add a "I'm stuck" function so the agent can explicitly give up

### For plan-and-execute

- Plan in a different model than execution (Claude Opus plans, Haiku executes)
- Validate the plan structurally (each step has clear inputs/outputs)
- Allow plan revision but cap revisions at 2-3
- Cache plan-to-execution mappings for recurring task types

### For multi-agent

- Pin role boundaries STRICTLY (researcher doesn't write, writer doesn't research)
- Use a deterministic orchestrator, not an LLM coordinator
- Set hard turn limits per agent (5 turns max, then handoff)
- Have ONE designated "final answer" agent — others can't ship
- Log inter-agent messages — they are the failure mode

## Framework picks

In 2026, three frameworks dominate:

**LangGraph** (LangChain): best general-purpose for state-machine-style agent control. Good for ReAct, plan-execute, and multi-agent. Strong typing, explicit graph definitions, good debugging tools.

**CrewAI**: easiest multi-agent setup. Role-based, opinionated. Production-friendly for content workflows. Less flexible than LangGraph.

**AutoGen** (Microsoft): research-grade multi-agent. Deep customization, dialog patterns, code execution loops. Heavier for production.

For single-agent ReAct, you don't really need a framework — Vercel AI SDK or raw OpenAI/Anthropic function calling is often enough.

## Common failure modes

**Agent loops with no progress.** Add a "Tools used this turn" counter. If the same tool is called 3+ times with similar args, force a different action.

**Multi-agent infinite back-and-forth.** Set strict turn limits. Default to "manager makes final call" when consensus fails.

**Plan that never adapts.** Plan-and-execute systems are brittle if environments change. Always allow replan on tool errors.

**Lost context in handoffs.** Multi-agent systems summarize between agents — summaries lose detail. For high-stakes tasks, pass FULL trajectory between agents, not summaries.

**Over-relying on the LLM for routing.** Hard rules (URL pattern, intent classifier output) beat LLM routing for predictable tasks.

## When to upgrade from single-agent

Signs you've outgrown single-agent ReAct:
- Tasks consistently take 15+ iterations
- Agent forgets earlier context mid-task
- You're spending most prompt tokens on tool definitions
- Specific sub-tasks need different system prompts than the main agent

Upgrade path: introduce a planner (plan-and-execute) BEFORE multi-agent. It's simpler, cheaper, and solves most "single-agent isn't enough" problems.

## Related open-source AI tools

- [LangGraph](/tool/langgraph-langchain-ai) — recommended for production agents
- [CrewAI](/tool/crewai-crewaiinc) — easiest multi-agent
- [AutoGen](/tool/autogen-microsoft) — research-grade multi-agent
- [Letta](/tool/letta-letta-ai) — long-running agent memory
- [Mem0](/tool/mem0-mem0ai) — agent memory store

## Related comparisons

- [LangGraph vs AutoGen](/compare/langgraph-langchain-ai-vs-autogen-microsoft)
- [AutoGen vs CrewAI](/compare/autogen-microsoft-vs-crewai-crewaiinc)

body_markdown:
# Prompt Engineering in 2026

Frontier models in 2026 are much better at following instructions than 2023 models. Most of what passed for prompt engineering then is now noise — bloated prompts that increase cost without improving output. This guide cuts to what actually moves the needle.

## What still works

### 1. Structured outputs (JSON mode, function calling)

The single highest-leverage technique. Define a schema, tell the model to produce JSON matching it. Modern models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5+, Gemini 1.5+) honor this rigorously.

```python
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o",
    messages=[...],
    response_format={"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": {...}}
)
```

Why it works: the model is forced into a constrained decoding path. No regex needed downstream. No "model gave me a weird format today" debugging at 2am.

### 2. Few-shot with 3-5 diverse examples

For any task with even mild ambiguity, show 3-5 examples in the prompt. Diversity matters more than count — 3 well-chosen examples beat 10 similar ones.

Pattern:
```
Here are examples of correctly answering customer support questions:

Q: How do I reset my password?
A: Click "Forgot password" at login. Email sent within 30 seconds.

Q: My order #12345 is missing.
A: Tracking shows delivered 2 days ago. Check with neighbors first. If still missing, reply and we'll refund.

Q: Can I get a refund?
A: Yes within 30 days. Reply with order number; refund hits the card in 3-5 business days.

Q: {USER_QUESTION}
A:
```

Frontier models are remarkably good at picking up the format, tone, and answer style from few-shot examples.

### 3. Explicit output format spec

When you don't use structured outputs, spell out the output format literally. Don't trust the model to infer it.

Bad:
```
Summarize the article.
```

Better:
```
Summarize the article in exactly 3 bullet points. Each bullet starts with a verb. Maximum 15 words per bullet.
```

The 2024+ models follow these constraints rigorously. The 2022 models struggled. Don't carry over your 2022 mistrust.

### 4. Chain-of-thought (only for hard reasoning)

Adding "Let's think step by step" before the answer reliably improves math, code, and multi-step reasoning. It does NOT improve everyday Q&A and DOES inflate token cost.

Rule: use CoT for tasks where you need the model to derive an answer through multiple inference steps. Skip CoT for retrieval-style tasks.

For very hard problems, sample N=8-32 CoT samples and majority-vote (self-consistency).

### 5. Prompt caching for stable prefixes

Anthropic and OpenAI both support prompt caching: cached input tokens cost 10-50% of normal. Structure your prompts so the system prompt + few-shot examples + RAG context comes FIRST (stable), then the user query LAST (variable).

Result: 5-10x cost reduction on repeat traffic with identical prefixes.

```
[STABLE: 8K tokens of system prompt + few-shot + RAG context]  ← cached
[VARIABLE: user query]                                          ← not cached
```

## What to stop doing

### 1. Stacking personas

"You are an expert software engineer with 30 years of experience and a PhD in computer science and you've worked at Google and Apple..."

Modern models don't need this. The first 5 words establish role; the rest is wasted tokens. "You are a senior backend engineer." is enough.

### 2. "You are a helpful AI assistant"

Already baked into RLHF. Saying it doesn't make it more so. Delete.

### 3. Exhaustive negative instructions

"Don't be verbose. Don't add caveats. Don't repeat the question. Don't say 'as an AI'. Don't use emoji unless asked. Don't..."

Each negative instruction is a hint to do that thing. Use ONE positive instruction: "Reply in 2-3 sentences, no preamble."

### 4. "Take a deep breath" / "Think carefully"

These tricks helped 2022-2023 models. In 2026 they're noise. The models don't have lungs. Use CoT for reasoning tasks; skip the theater.

### 5. Anchoring constraints inside long prompts

"By the way, please respond in JSON" buried in paragraph 4 of an 800-word system prompt gets ignored. Critical constraints belong at the TOP (sticky) or BOTTOM (recency).

## The structure that works

Default prompt structure for 2026 frontier models:

```
[ROLE — 1 short line]
You are a senior software engineer reviewing pull requests.

[TASK — 1-2 lines]
Review the diff below. Flag bugs, suggest improvements, approve if it ships.

[FEW-SHOT — 3-5 examples if format is non-obvious]
[Examples here]

[INPUT — clearly delimited]
DIFF:
{diff_content}

[OUTPUT FORMAT — explicit]
Return JSON: { "verdict": "approve" | "request-changes", "issues": [{ "line": N, "comment": "..." }] }
```

Total: usually 200-500 tokens. Not 2000.

## Tasks where prompt engineering won't save you

Some failures aren't prompt problems:

- **Hallucination on facts the model doesn't know** → use RAG
- **Inconsistent output format** → use structured outputs
- **Wrong knowledge cutoff** → use RAG with fresh data
- **Need specific brand voice** → fine-tune
- **Multi-step reasoning beyond 5 steps** → break into separate calls

Throwing more prompt tokens at these doesn't help.

## Debug your prompts like code

Build an eval set of 20-100 representative inputs with expected outputs. Run your prompt through them. Score automatically (exact match, regex, LLM-as-judge for soft signals).

When you change a prompt, re-run the eval. If quality drops 5%+, roll back. Don't ship prompts by vibes.

## Tools that actually help

- **OpenAI Playground / Anthropic Console**: iterate prompts quickly with side-by-side comparison
- **promptfoo**: open-source eval harness, runs your prompt against a test set and scores
- **LangSmith / Langfuse**: trace production prompts, diff versions
- **Helicone**: prompt logging + caching layer for OpenAI/Anthropic APIs

## The boring truth

Most of what made 2022 prompts ugly was working around model weakness. 2026 models are good. Write prompts like you'd write a clear instruction to a junior teammate: state the role, give 3 examples, specify output format, hand over the input.

The temptation to add "JSON only, no preamble, do not include explanations, ALWAYS validate, NEVER hallucinate" is a tell that you're prompting like it's 2023. Trust the model. Test the prompt. Ship.

## Related open-source AI tools

- [promptfoo](/tool/promptfoo) — open-source prompt eval harness
- [DSPy](/tool/dspy-stanfordnlp) — programmatic prompt optimization
- [LangSmith](/tool/langsmith-langchain-ai) — prompt observability
- [Instructor](/tool/instructor-library) — pydantic-based structured outputs

## Related comparisons

- [Promptfoo vs DeepEval](/compare/promptfoo-vs-deepeval-confident-ai)
- [LangChain vs LlamaIndex](/compare/langchain-langchain-ai-vs-llama-index-run-llama)
